The incubation period of the Red-throated bee-eater (Merops bulocki) has been documented under controlled conditions, with eggs held at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] requiring approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days] to hatch. This developmental duration aligns with the range of three to four weeks reported for the European bee-eater, Merops apiaster, and suggests a conserved thermal sensitivity within the genus. Newly emerged nestlings, termed altricial chicks at the point of first feeding, are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams]. This modest initial mass underscores the considerable parental investment required to shepherd the brood through the subsequent nestling phase, a period characterized by rapid feather development and somatic growth as the chicks transition from complete dependence on crop milk and insect prey to a diet of aerial arthropods delivered by both parents.

Throughout the nestling period, the developing chicks experience a phase of rapid mass gain, ultimately reaching a full adult body mass of 34.8 grams [Wwi = 34.8 grams], representing their stable adult weight. This value, consistent with measurements taken from the congener Merops bullockoides, indicates the species achieves a relatively modest size for an avian insectivore. The transition from a hatchling mass of only 2.5 grams to this adult size involves a near fourteen-fold increase in body mass, a trajectory that demands a high provisioning rate from the breeding adults. Field records show that nestlings begin to exhibit flight feather maturation and will eventually fledge from the burrow nest, marking the point of first flight achievement and the onset of nutritional independence from their parents.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active breeding season for this species, which often sees ambient temperatures reaching 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the progression of key life-history milestones follows a predictable schedule. The time since birth at fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, is approximately 21 days since birth [tx = approximately 21 days since birth] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of many bee-eaters and is likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk in the nesting burrow. Following fledging, the immature bird, now a juvenile, enters a sub-adult phase where it must hone its aerial hunting skills while still being provisioned intermittently by the adults before achieving full independence and beginning to forage on its own.

Sexual maturation in the Red-throated bee-eater is reached relatively quickly after fledging, paralleling the pace observed in related species. In an environment where ambient conditions hover around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty is documented as 63 days since birth [tp = 63 days since birth]. This rapid attainment of gonadal activity allows young birds to potentially contribute to the breeding population within the same season they hatched, although in practice, many individuals may defer their first breeding attempt. The first reproduction event, or time since birth at first brood, occurs at approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth], typically aligning with the following breeding season at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delay reflects the time required for juveniles to fully develop foraging proficiency and establish the burrow territories essential for successful reproduction.

The lifespan of this species, as inferred from records on the related Merops bullockoides maintained under warm conditions, suggests a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when living at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Given this extended lifespan and the rapid maturation schedule, a breeding pair can produce multiple broods over several seasons. The maximum reproductive rate, realized under the same thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], amounts to approximately 6 eggs per year, a figure consistent with a strategy of small clutches repeated across the breeding season. This combination of modest fecundity per event but high event frequency aligns with the species' life-history strategy of sustaining a relatively high annual output while minimizing the energetic burden on any single brood.
